T-GADE: Thermodynamical Generative-AI-Driven
Evolution of LLM Artifacts
Kyoko Ogawa and Naoki Mori
Abstract—Introducing large language models (LLMs) into evo-
lutionary computation enables semantic generation of candidates,
but the classical problem of maintaining population diversity
remains. Inspired by the thermodynamical genetic algorithm
(TDGA), we propose T-GADE (Thermodynamical Generative-AI-
Driven Evolution of LLM Artifacts), an evolutionary computation
framework extended through LLMs. T-GADE keeps the notions
of a population and genetic operators, takes structured artifacts
generated by an LLM as individuals, and implements crossover
and mutation as LLM operators. It further introduces the
HoxLM, an LLM that attempts self-repair of an individual after
evaluation and before survival selection; two update schemes,
generational and steady-state; and Fermi-type and Bose-type oc-
cupancy rules that define solution identity and whether duplicates
are permitted. Survival selection is unified as minimization of
the free energy FT = ⟨E⟩−TH, and the selection temperature
T explicitly controls the balance between quality and diversity.
We tested an implementation example aligned with Evolution of
Heuristics (EoH) on the online bin-packing task, where the excess
is the bin count in excess of the volume lower bound, relative to
that bound. The HoxLM-equipped configuration reached lower
excess with fewer total LLM calls than EoH. In the preregistered
comparison at 400 total calls it won 9 of 10 seed-paired runs, with
a median sealed excess of 0.836% against 3.912%, and it was also
better in the mean and in the worst case. Temperature controls
the spread of the retained population under both update schemes,
and a small positive temperature improves training quality over
the collapsed T = 0 point in the generational Bose-type scheme.
The evolved heuristics are shown as readable scoring rules.
Index Terms—Evolutionary computation, large language mod-
els, thermodynamical selection, diversity control, program evo-
lution.
I. INTRODUCTION
With the development of large language models (LLMs),
problem-solving methods that combine several models or gen-
erated outputs have been studied. Evolutionary computation
keeps several candidate solutions as a population and searches
through genetic operators and selection. Semantic modification
of candidates by an LLM and the coverage of a population
are complementary, so evolutionary computation also applies
to search over natural language and programs [1], [2], [3].
Studies that combine the two can be organized from three
perspectives: (1) evolutionary optimization of LLM weights
or structure; (2) LLMs in genetic operators or fitness evalua-
tion; and (3) LLMs or their outputs as evolving individuals.
Perspectives (2) and (3) concern the role of the LLM and the
object of evolution, respectively, and they are not mutually
K. Ogawa and N. Mori are with the Graduate School of Informatics,
Osaka Metropolitan University, Osaka, Japan (e-mail: si26145c@st.omu.ac.jp;
mnao@omu.ac.jp).
exclusive. We adopt (2) and (3): an LLM implements the ge-
netic operators, and its structured outputs form the individuals.
Fitness comes from a task-specific evaluator, which may be a
numerical evaluation or a judgment by an LLM.
In evolutionary computation, premature convergence has
long shown the importance of population diversity. Even with
an LLM, the evolution of artifacts requires explicit diversity
design. In particular, artifacts with different expressions may
show the same behavior. The questions are therefore what to
quantify as diversity, how much of it is appropriate, and how
to reflect it in survival selection. Many LLM-driven program
searches answer the last question implicitly, through a fixed
truncation rule or an island layout. We instead build a new
selection rule that treats diversity explicitly as a controlled
quantity.
Against this background, we propose T-GADE (Thermody-
namical Generative-AI-Driven Evolution of LLM Artifacts), a
diversity-aware framework for LLM-based evolutionary com-
putation. T-GADE is based on the thermodynamical genetic
algorithm (TDGA), which balances quality and population
diversity through a temperature [4]. T-GADE extends its free-
energy principle to LLM-based genetic operators and artifact-
level diversity functions, separating representation, evaluation,
and variation from survival selection. Artifacts are not limited
to code, and the evaluator and the diversity features are
defined per problem. Population update schemes include the
generational replacement model, which replaces the parent
population as a whole, and steady-state models, which replace
one or a few individuals per step [5], [6], [7]. The minimal
generation gap model, for example, replaces two parents
per step; the steady-state update of T-GADE replaces one
individual. Below we abbreviate the two schemes as genera-
tional and steady-state. The two differ in how fast individuals
turn over, but T-GADE treats both with one objective. We
adopt Fermi-type and Bose-type occupancy, named after single
occupation in Fermi–Dirac statistics and repeated occupation
in Bose–Einstein statistics. These rules make explicit how
many identical individuals may occupy the population. Update
scheme, occupancy, and temperature are independent design
choices. The experiments in this paper examine the temper-
ature sensitivity of performance within two fixed families,
steady-state Fermi-type and generational Bose-type.
For validation we use an implementation example of T-
GADE aligned with Evolution of Heuristics (EoH) [8], which
evolves explanations paired with executable heuristics. The
comparison uses the online bin-packing task of the EoH
paper. Under common filtering and tie-breaking, steady-state
Fermi-type T-GADE reproduces the survival rule of EoH at
arXiv:2609.12286v2  [cs.AI]  14 Oct 2026


--- Page 2 ---
2
zero temperature, so EoH’s survival rule is one point of the
framework. In the implementation example every child carries
a HoxLM, whose calls are charged to the same budget as
operator calls, so comparisons are made at equal total calls.
Our main contributions are the following four.
1) A free-energy framework, T-GADE, with three axes:
update scheme, occupancy, and temperature. It is a
general proposal that does not restrict the type of artifact
or the evaluator. The survival rule of EoH is the steady-
state Fermi-type point at T = 0, and generational Bose-
type selection at T = 0 is a collapse to copies. We
state the conditions under which one-member removal
is exact and prove both zero-temperature propositions.
2) In an implementation example aligned with EoH, a
HoxLM-equipped configuration reaches low excess with
fewer total calls than EoH. The preregistered primary
comparison at 400 total calls confirms this with 9 wins
in 10 seed pairs (p = 0.0039), and the configuration
is better in median, mean, and worst case. This con-
figuration is the EoH survival rule at T
= 0 with
the HoxLM attached, so the preregistered comparison
isolates the HoxLM; the diversity control by temperature
is the second instrument of T-GADE and is assessed in
the temperature-response experiments.
3) The temperature response of both families at seven
temperatures. The spread of the retained population rises
with T in both families. Training quality has its best
median at T = 0 in the steady-state Fermi-type family
and at T = 0.001 in the generational Bose-type family.
The generational T = 0 point is a control whose collapse
Proposition 1 predicts. The gain of T = 0.001 over this
control is significant on training excess and a descriptive
trend on the sealed c100 instances, and the favorable
region extends descriptively to T = 0.003.
4) A concrete account of what was evolved. Two heuristics
traced from seeds fixed in advance are shown with their
scoring rules and a placement example. In the lineage of
improvements at intermediate temperatures, more than
half descend from non-best survivors.
II. RELATED WORK
A. LLMs and evolutionary computation
For perspective (1), evolutionary model merging searches
weights and information flow among pretrained models to
construct a new model [9]. The following discussion focuses
on perspectives (2) and (3): LLMs as components of search
and generated artifacts as individuals.
Evolution through Large Models mutates programs with an
LLM [1]; EvoPrompt evolves natural-language prompts [2];
Promptbreeder evolves prompts and mutation instructions [3].
These methods make meaningful descriptions material for
inheritance and variation.
For program evolution, FunSearch links LLM proposals
with execution-based evaluation and an island-based program
database [10]. EoH represents a heuristic through its explana-
tion and code [8]; ReEvo uses reflection on evaluation results
to guide subsequent proposals [11]. LLaMEA generates, mod-
ifies, and selects metaheuristics using execution feedback [12].
The HoxLM of T-GADE also feeds evaluation results back to
an LLM, but it acts within one individual and leaves survival to
the free energy. In memetic-algorithm terms, the HoxLM is a
Lamarckian local-improvement step applied to each individual
before survival selection.
B. Exploration and diversity control
HSEvo uses diversity measurements and Harmony Search
for improvement [13]. MCTS-AHD organizes generated
heuristics in a search tree and continues refinement from
intermediate candidates [14]. EoH-S evolves complementary
sets of heuristics and evaluates the best member for each
instance [15]. LLM-LNS evolves heuristic strategies and the
prompts that guide their evolution, addressing diversity on the
generation side [16].
Novelty Search selects for behavioral novelty [17], and
MAP-Elites retains high-quality solutions across regions of a
behavior space [18]. In-context QD uses a diverse archive to
condition LLM generation [19]. Determinantal point processes
use similarity information to favor diverse subsets [20]; the
log-determinant diversity of T-GADE is of this kind.
TDGA incorporates population entropy into a temperature-
weighted objective for survival selection [4]. Adaptation to
changing environments and temperature control through Feed-
back TDGA have also been studied [21], [22]; the present
work uses fixed temperatures and measures their effect. T-
GADE extends this lineage to evolutionary computation with
LLM-based genetic operators, artifact-level diversity, and ex-
plicit occupancy rules.
III. T-GADE
A. Individuals and evaluation
T-GADE treats structured artifacts generated by an LLM
as individuals. An artifact is any LLM output with explicit
structure, such as a description paired with code, a natural-
language plan, or a design proposal; below we simply write
artifact. The LLM generates initial individuals from a task
specification and generates children from evaluated parents. A
task-specific evaluator assigns an energy E(x) to individual x;
lower is better. The evaluator may be a numerical evaluation
such as an execution result, or a judgment by an LLM (LLM-
as-a-judge). Diversity is designed per problem. Feature vectors
ϕℓ(x), ℓ= 1, . . . , m, measure differences between artifacts,
and their choice determines what counts as diversity. Artifacts
are inherited from parent to child; features are measured after
generation.
B. Genetic operators
Genetic operators are implemented as instructions to the
LLM. Crossover generates a new artifact from the artifacts of
several parents; mutation generates one from a single parent.
The design of the operators depends on the task and on the
artifact format, and T-GADE is not restricted to particular
instruction texts. Variation is independent of survival selection,
and the method of sampling parents is also a design choice.


--- Page 3 ---
3
C. Free-energy minimization
Survival selection in T-GADE combines quality and di-
versity into one quantity and minimizes it, so that high-
quality individuals survive and the survivors differ from one
another. The minimum-free-energy principle describes thermal
equilibrium under fixed constraints by
F = ⟨E⟩−TH,
(1)
where ⟨E⟩is mean energy, H is entropy, and T is temperature.
TDGA applies this principle to population selection: mean
energy measures fitness, and entropy computed from allele
frequencies measures population diversity [4]. T-GADE retains
this quality–diversity balance while defining diversity over
artifacts.
Let N be the target population size and P a nonempty
population of size n = |P|. Repeated copies count as separate
individuals. H(P) is a population diversity measure; in this
paper we use the log-determinant of the Gram matrix of the
feature vectors. Let Xℓ(P) contain the feature vectors as rows,
and define Gℓ(P) = Xℓ(P)Xℓ(P)⊤. We define
FT (P) = ⟨E⟩P −TH(P),
⟨E⟩P = 1
n
X
x∈P
E(x),
H(P) = 1
n
m
X
ℓ=1
log det(Gℓ(P) + εIn) .
(2)
Here T ≥0, ε > 0 regularizes the Gram matrix, and In is
the identity matrix. With normalized features and fixed size, H
measures joint artifact diversity per individual. The framework
does not fix the features ϕℓ: they are quantitative features
chosen per problem, and H is then determined by their Gram
matrices. Examples are a recorded execution behavior for exe-
cutable artifacts, used in this paper, an embedding of the output
for text artifacts, and, with a self-hosted open-weight gen-
erator, its intermediate-layer representations. With unit-norm
features, Hadamard’s inequality gives H(P) ≤m log(1 + ε).
Unlike Shannon entropy, this log-volume measure can be
negative. Selection uses quality alone at T = 0 and includes
diversity at T > 0. The selection temperature T weights this
deterministic trade-off, and its numerical scale depends on the
energy and feature scales and on ε. The selection temperature
is a parameter of survival selection and is distinct from the
sampling temperature that sets the randomness of LLM output.
D. Fermi-type and Bose-type occupancy
Single occupation in Fermi–Dirac statistics and repeated
occupation in Bose–Einstein statistics motivate two population
rules. Fermi-type occupancy permits at most one individual per
level; Bose-type occupancy permits repeated occupation. The
equivalence criterion of a level is defined per problem. A level
may be the identity of the artifact itself, or the identity of the
recorded objective value. The former excludes only duplicates
of the same solution; the latter keeps one solution per quality
value.
Generational Bose-type selection may select the same can-
didate repeatedly to fill population slots. Steady-state Bose-
type selection admits duplicates already in its input; it does

E. Generational update
The generational scheme freezes the parent population,
proposes several children, and constructs a new population
from evaluated parents and children. Here, N parents and
N +1 proposed children form the candidate pool Q. Selection
gives priority to quality and first takes a minimum-energy
candidate. Each subsequent addition minimizes
∆FT (y | P) = FT (P ⊎{y}) −FT (P)
= E(y) −T Pm
ℓ=1 log dℓ(y) −FT (P)
n + 1
.
(3)
Here n = |P| ≥1, dℓ(y) is the Schur complement in Ap-
pendix C, and ⊎counts a selected copy as another individual.
For a fixed prefix, minimizing (3) is equivalent to minimizing
E(y) −T P
ℓlog dℓ(y). This is the marginal cost of nFT (P),
the greedy step of a log-determinant regularized objective [20].
Fermi-type selection excludes every candidate at the selected
level from subsequent additions; Bose-type selection leaves
candidates available.
def greedy_survivors(pool, N, T, fermi_type):
available = list(pool)
first = min(available, key=energy)
selected, state = [first], SchurState([first])
if fermi_type:
remove_level(available, first)
while len(selected) < N:
def cost(x):
# gain(x) = sum_l log d_l(x)
return energy(x) - T * state.gain(x)
child = min(available, key=cost)
selected.append(child)
state.add(child)
# rank-one update of R_l
if fermi_type:
remove_level(available, child)
return materialize_copies(selected)
Planning assigns parents and operators before parallel gen-
eration; results enter in plan order. Invalid candidates are
excluded, and minima preserve input order on ties. Fermi-type

4
selection assumes that the candidate pool contains at least N
distinct admissible levels. As Appendix C shows, given feature
inner products, the Schur complement evaluates each diversity
increment in O(|P|2) operations per block. In the pseudocode,
state holds the inverses Rℓ, which the released generational
implementation (free_energy.py) updates after each pick
by the rank-one formula (10). Exact selection of N individuals
requires combinatorial search, which motivates the greedy
construction; a global approximation guarantee remains future
work.
Proposition 1 (Zero-temperature collapse). Under Bose-type
occupancy at T
=
0, with ties broken by input order,
the generational construction returns N copies of the first
minimum-energy candidate.
Proof. At T = 0 the cost of every candidate is E(y) up to the
common term, so each step selects the same minimum-energy
candidate, which Bose-type occupancy leaves available.
Because the parents are part of the pool Q, this collapse is
reached after the first update and persists, since the copies are
the parents of every later child. Zero temperature is therefore
a boundary of the generational Bose-type family rather than a
reference method.
F. Steady-state update
The steady-state scheme updates the population whenever a
new candidate finishes evaluation. Each asynchronous child
generation, that is, one operator call, uses the population
available at its start. Registrations, that is, admissions of
evaluated candidates to the update, are serialized in order of
evaluation completion. A new individual is also eligible for
removal.
Candidates are first filtered by the occupancy rule: the first
candidate per level is kept under Fermi-type occupancy, and no
deduplication is applied under Bose-type occupancy. If more
than N candidates remain, the update removes the individual
that minimizes the free energy of the survivors:
x∗∈arg min
x∈Q FT (Q \ {x}).
(4)
Ties in survivor free energy are broken by removing the
larger objective first and then the later arrival. At positive
temperature, candidates without valid features are excluded
first, and removal among the remaining candidates is chosen
by quality and feature overlap. If fewer than N candidates
remain, all are retained.
Proposition 2 (One-member removal). Fix a pool of N + 1
labeled individuals for which every one-member removal is
admissible. Rule (4) minimizes free energy over all its N-
member subpopulations.
Proof. Each N-member subpopulation is the complement of
exactly one labeled individual. The rule compares all such
complements.
G. HoxLM
An individual in T-GADE may carry a HoxLM. The HoxLM
is an LLM that acts after the evaluation of the individual and
before survival selection; it reads the evaluation result and
attempts a self-repair of that individual’s artifact. The repaired
proposal is evaluated again, and an adoption rule decides
whether it replaces the original individual or the original is
kept unchanged. Unlike the genetic operators, the HoxLM
acts within one individual and takes no part in composing the
population. Survival is left to the free energy. HoxLM calls
are counted as LLM calls in the same way as operator calls.
H. Meaning of zero temperature
At T = 0 free-energy minimization reduces to mean-energy
minimization, but its behavior differs with the combination
of update scheme and occupancy. In the steady-state Fermi-
type family, exclusion per level remains, so zero temperature
removes the worst individual and can coincide with an ex-
isting quality-only selection rule. In the generational Bose-
type family nothing prevents copies, so zero temperature is a
collapse, as Proposition 1 states. Statements about T-GADE at
zero temperature must therefore name the family.
IV. COMPARISON METHOD AND IMPLEMENTATION
EXAMPLE
This section describes one implementation example that
makes T-GADE concrete for comparison with EoH; it is not
the definition of T-GADE.
A. Comparison method: EoH
EoH [8] represents a heuristic as a natural-language expla-
nation (thought) paired with executable code and generates
children with four prompt templates, E1, E2, M1, and M2. Its
population management excludes failed evaluations, keeps the
first candidate at each recorded objective value, and retains at
most N candidates in ascending objective order. The EoH arm
of this paper, arm A, runs the EoH algorithm with its released
operator templates and evaluator inside the same steady-state
loop as the T-GADE arms, with the same model and initial
population, and without the HoxLM.
B. Example task
We use the online bin-packing task of the EoH paper. Items
arrive sequentially and cannot be reassigned. The scoring
function assigns a score to every bin whose available capacity
admits the item, including unused bins, and the item goes to
the bin with the maximum score. Ties go to the lowest-index
bin, and fewer used bins are better. Training uses the five
Weibull instances of the EoH release, each with capacity 100
and 5,000 items; an item size is 45 times a Weibull variate of
shape 3, clipped to [1, 100]. For instance j, let Bj(x) be the
number of bins used by program x, and let Lj be the volume
lower bound, the total item size divided by the bin capacity
and rounded up. The training excess ratio is
r(x) =
P5
j=1[Bj(x) −Lj]
P5
j=1 Lj
.
(5)


--- Page 5 ---
5
The excess ratio, or excess for short, is the ratio of the bin-
count excess to the lower bound; lower is better.
Two sets of sealed instances, five each with capacity 100
(c100) and capacity 500 (c500), are generated from recorded
seeds with the same item distribution, rounded and clipped
to [1, 100], with 5,000 items per instance. The instances are
hash-sealed, and the seeds and hashes are in the repository.
They are never read during search or by any prompt, and
they are scored only after all runs have finished. Sealed excess
averages the instance-wise ratios [Bj(x) −Lj]/Lj. The c100
set confirms training results on the training distribution; the
c500 set measures transfer to another capacity.
C. Implementation of T-GADE
An individual is an explanation paired with code, as in
EoH, and its evaluation record comprises the behavior and the
objective value obtained by execution on the training instances.
The energy is
E(x) = min(r(x), 2)
2
.
(6)
A generated program runs in isolation with a 30-second
timeout, and a lexical gate rejects random-number APIs.
Diversity uses one L2-normalized, 10,000-dimensional fea-
ture vector formed by concatenating fill ratio and tightness
rank over 5,000 placement decisions on the first training
instance, with ε = 0.001. This compares placement behavior
on the same sequence of item arrivals; extending it to all
five instances is a straightforward variant. Behavior rather
than code is used because different code can show the same
behavior, and such surface differences should not count as
diversity. Fill ratio is the occupancy of the chosen bin after
placement. Tightness rank is the position of the chosen bin
among the feasible bins sorted by ascending available capacity,
normalized to [0, 1], where 0 is the tightest bin and 1 is the
emptiest bin.
For a fair comparison, the operators reuse the four EoH
templates. E1 proposes an algorithm different in form from
two parents. E2 uses their shared idea to create a different
form. M1 changes one parent’s structure; M2 changes its
parameters. Each prompt supplies parent explanations and
code and requests a new explanation and code. Operators are
chosen with equal probability, and parents are sampled with
probability proportional to 1/(rank+N) by quality rank, as in
EoH. All arms start from the same initial population of eight
individuals, generated once beforehand from a fixed seed and
not charged to the call budget.
A level is identified by the training excess ratio r(x)
rounded to five decimal places. Under Fermi-type occupancy,
two individuals with equal objective and different code occupy
the same level, and only one of them is retained. Under this
definition, the survival rule of EoH, which keeps the first
candidate at each recorded objective value, is a Fermi-type
rule. The experiments use the steady-state Fermi-type and
generational Bose-type combinations.
The scale of T can be read from the regularization. For a
retained set consisting of k copies of one unit vector, the Schur
complement (8) of one more copy is ε(k + 1 + ε)/(k + ε),
about 2ε for k = 1 and tending to ε as k grows. Adding
the first copy of a retained individual therefore contributes
log(2ε) ≈−6.2 to the log-determinant with ε = 10−3,
whereas adding a distinct, nearly orthogonal individual con-
tributes about log(1 + ε) ≈0. In this illustration a copy
therefore pays a diversity penalty of about 6.2T energy units.
In the unclipped range r < 2 of (6), this is about 1240T
percentage points of excess: 0.4 points at T = 0.0003, 1.2
points at T = 0.001, 3.7 points at T = 0.003, and 124 points
at T = 0.1. This rule of thumb locates the temperatures used
below relative to the quality differences within the population.
Below we call the HoxLM of this implementation the host.
The host acts on a proposed child after its evaluation and
before its registration, as one improve step. Its prompt contains
a hand-written domain card with bin-packing knowledge,
including summary statistics of the training item distribution.
It also contains the function interface, the child’s measured
training excess, an execution probe that reports tied placements
on a short item sequence, the code and value of the best parent,
and the child itself. The host returns one revised explanation
and code with a single change. If the code changed, the revised
program is evaluated again, and the revision is adopted only
if it passes the validity checks and strictly improves training
energy. Otherwise the original child is registered unchanged.
We call this adoption rule the keep-best rule; no child is
dropped. There are two exceptions. First, a revision that
changes only the explanation is adopted with the energy of
the original child, since the code is unchanged. Second, if the
original child failed evaluation, a valid revision is adopted.
The host is the only LLM that sees training values and the
domain card.
Calls are counted as the sum of operator calls and host
calls. One host call per child is charged to the budget, so a
host-equipped run with 1,600 operator calls uses at most 3,200
calls, the same as the EoH reference. Since the host is common
to every host-equipped arm, temperature comparisons within
a family are internal to the host-equipped design.
D. Relation to EoH
Proposition 3 (Zero-temperature identity). For the same or-
dered candidates, failure filtering, and first-per-level filtering,
suppose energy is a nondecreasing function of objective. In
exact arithmetic, steady-state Fermi-type selection at T = 0
returns the same ordered survivors as EoH, provided energy
ties remove the larger objective first and output is sorted by
objective.
Proof. At zero temperature, minimizing the mean energy
of a fixed-size survivor population is equivalent to remov-
ing a worst individual. Objective-based tie-breaking resolves
plateaus of the energy map. Repetition leaves the lowest
objective values, and stable output ordering gives the same
result.
T-GADE in this implementation thus contains the survival
rule of EoH as the steady-state Fermi-type point at zero
temperature. The identity holds for common input and does not
guarantee identical search trajectories. Together with Proposi-
tion 1, it shows that T = 0 is a reference method in one family


--- Page 6 ---
6
and a degenerate boundary in the other; the two families must
be read separately.
V. EXPERIMENTAL CONDITIONS
A. Model and common conditions
All runs use the open-weight model gpt-oss-20b [23] (Ope-
nAI; 21 B total and 3.6 B active parameters) served by the
vLLM inference engine [24] on one self-hosted GPU. The
marginal cost of a call is therefore zero, and no provider-
side change can occur during the experiments. The operator
output limit is 2,048 tokens and the host limit is 8,192 tokens;
the LLM sampling temperature is 0.8. The population size is
N = 8. The steady-state loop uses two LLM-call workers and
two evaluation workers; the generational loop uses four of each
and plans parent and operator assignments before dispatch.
B. Design and preregistration
Table I shows the experimental design. Each configuration
is run once per seed. The temperature response of the steady-
state Fermi-type family compares EoH with 3,200 operator
calls against T-GADE with 1,600 operator calls plus at most
one host call per child, at seven temperatures. The tempera-
ture response of the generational Bose-type family runs 177
generations of 9 operator and 9 host calls, that is, 3,186
calls. The reach-speed experiment compares EoH with 800
operator calls against host-equipped Fermi-type T-GADE with
400 operator calls plus at most 400 host calls, at T = 0
and T = 0.003. Every experiment was preregistered before
launch with its arms, seeds, endpoints, and tests, and the
registrations are distributed with the code. The preregistered
primary comparison reported in this paper is B against A
at 400 total calls in the seed group 86001–86010, and all
other comparisons are treated as secondary. In the generational
Bose-type family, T = 0 is a control condition: Proposition 1
predicts its collapse to copies, so the question is whether a
small positive temperature restores a diverse population and
better quality.
C. Budget points and endpoints
To compare runs with different call structures, we evaluate
the budget-point selection at b ∈{200, 400, 800, 1600} total
calls and at the endpoint. For the steady-state loop, the scorer
counts, for each registration, the operator and host requests
started before its registration time. The budget-point selection
is then the best training individual among registrations whose
count does not exceed b. For the generational loop it is the
history-best individual, that is, the best training individual
registered so far, up to generation ⌊b/18⌋; this conversion
is nominal because failed operator calls leave vacancies. The
endpoint is the history-best individual. Selection always uses
training values; sealed values are reported for the selected
individual and are never used for selection.
D. Statistical comparison
The unit of analysis is one run. For each arm we report
the median, mean, standard deviation, best, and worst over
the ten seeds. The best value is a single-run extreme and
is given as a reference only. Comparisons within the same
seed group are paired by seed and use the two-sided exact
Wilcoxon signed-rank test; for the temperature grid, the six
comparisons against T
= 0 at one budget point form a
family for Holm adjustment. The p values in the tables are
rounded to three decimals; the Holm-adjusted values in the
text are computed from the full-precision p values. Trends
over the seven temperatures are described by Spearman’s rank
correlation of the arm summaries against the temperature rank.
Training, sealed c100, and sealed c500 results are reported
separately.
VI. RESULTS
A. Reach speed against EoH
Table II and Fig. 2(b) show the reach-speed comparison.
At the primary endpoint of 400 total calls, the host-equipped
Fermi-type arm at T = 0 (B) outperformed the EoH arm
(A) in 9 of 10 seed pairs (p = 0.0039). The median sealed
excess is 0.836% against 3.912%, and B is also better in the
mean and in the worst run. Arm C has the smallest dispersion
at 400 calls and the best endpoint median and worst value
of the three arms, but its difference from B is a secondary,
unadjusted comparison. Because arm B at T = 0 is EoH’s
survival rule with the host attached, the difference between
B and A measures the host under equal total calls, not the
diversity term.
In Fig. 2(a) the host-equipped arms also reach a sealed
median below 1% by 400 total calls, whereas EoH needs
about 1,600 calls. The claim of this paper is that the tested
configuration reaches lower sealed excess at the same number
of total LLM calls on this task and model, although the host-
equipped runs use about 1.7 times the tokens per call.
B. Temperature response
Table III and Fig. 3 give the endpoint results of the two
families at the seven temperatures; Table IV and Fig. 4 give
the diversity of the retained population. Temperature controls
the spread of the retained population in both families, and the
two families respond differently in quality.
In the steady-state Fermi-type family, T = 0, which is the
EoH survival rule with the host attached, is the best point. The
median training excess is 0.508%, the mean 0.531%, and the
worst 0.644%, and the median sealed c100 excess is 0.672%.
Training excess degrades slowly as the temperature rises; the
Spearman correlation over the seven medians is ρ = +0.89.
There are small non-monotone steps between T = 0.0003 and
0.003. After Holm adjustment only the highest temperature,
T = 0.1, differs significantly from T = 0, with 0 wins in
10, p = 0.002, and adjusted 0.012. The sealed c100 values
do not separate at any temperature. The EoH reference at the
same total calls has a training median of 0.624% and a sealed
median of 0.711%. The host-equipped T = 0 arm is better or

The generational Bose-type family responds differently. As
Proposition 1 states, the population collapses to copies at
T = 0, and every run ends with eight copies of one individual.
This point is the predicted control, not a tuned configura-
tion. The median training excess improves only slowly, from
0.649% at 800 calls to 0.644% at 1,600 calls and 0.614% at the
endpoint. A small positive temperature restores a population of
distinct survivors and improves quality. T = 0.001 has the best
training median of the generational grid, 0.548%, and the best
sealed c100 median, 0.652%. Against T = 0, T = 0.001 wins
10 of 10 seed pairs on training excess, with p = 0.002 and
Holm-adjusted 0.012, and 9 of 10 on the sealed instances, with
p = 0.014 and adjusted 0.082. At T = 0.003 the wins are 8 of
9 decided pairs on training (p = 0.023, adjusted 0.117) and 7
of 10 on the sealed instances (p = 0.027, adjusted 0.137), so
T = 0.003 does not separate from T = 0 after adjustment. The
two temperatures do not separate from each other (p = 0.31).
Descriptively, the favorable region is T = 0.001–0.003; its
significance rests on the training excess at T = 0.001. On the
sealed c100 instances the same gain is a descriptive trend that
does not reach significance after Holm adjustment (0.082).
From T = 0.01 upward the population becomes diversity-
heavy and the training endpoint returns to the level of T = 0.
In the units of Section IV-C, this region corresponds to a copy

Fig. 3. Temperature response of the two families. Each point is the median over 10 seed-paired runs; bars show the interquartile range, and the two series are
offset horizontally for readability. T = 0 is a separate category and is joined by a dotted segment; the positive temperatures sit at approximately log-spaced
categorical positions. The gray lines in (a) mark the EoH reference with 3,200 operator calls on the same seeds (training median 0.624, sealed c100 median
0.711). The steady-state family (a) is best at T = 0 and degrades slowly with temperature; the generational family (b) collapses at T = 0 and is best between

penalty of 1.2 to 3.7 percentage points. This is about one
order of magnitude above the objective spread of the retained
population, 0.15 to 0.37 points in Table IV.
Table IV shows what the temperature changes. The objective
spread of the final population rises monotonically with T
in both families (Spearman ρ = +1.0), from 0.10 to 3.6
percentage points in the steady-state family and from 0 to
3.9 points in the generational family. Code distance and the
number of distinct lexical code patterns also rise overall. In
the generational family the number of distinct individuals
among the eight survivors, averaged over generations, rises
from 1.0 at T = 0 to 6.2 at T = 0.0003 and saturates near 8
from T = 0.001. The temperature is thus a working control
of retained diversity, and the intermediate points of the grid
behave consistently with their neighbors.
On the sealed c500 instances, which test transfer to capacity
500, the medians lie between 0.37% and 1.54% and separate
no temperature or family, and the distributions have heavy
tails. We therefore make no transfer claim.
C. What was evolved
The numbers above summarize scoring functions that can
be read directly. We trace two individuals, fixed in advance by
seed and selected by training value only.
The first is the final best of generational Bose-type T-GADE
at T = 0.003 on seed 85001, with training excess 0.503%. Let
C be the bin capacity, a ≤C the available capacity of a bin
before the item is placed, δ = a −item the residual capacity
after placement, and i the zero-based position of the bin among
the feasible bins. The sum below runs over the feasible bins

It rewards an exact fit and otherwise prefers a residual near 40
with a Gaussian of width 15; it suppresses residuals below 15
linearly, because such bins cannot be reused by most items,
and favors earlier bins. For an item of size 40 and feasible bins
with available capacity a of 44, 80, and 100, the scores are
2.7×10−4, 8.9×10−2, and 3.7×10−2. The heuristic therefore
places the item in the bin with 80, leaving a reusable residual
of 40, rather than in the best-fit bin with 44, which would
leave an unusable residual of 4. Its explanation records that
the suppression threshold was changed from 30 to 15. This
is a parameter change of the M2 type that the host adopted
because it improved training excess. Its provenance illustrates
the use of retained candidates. It was produced in generation
128 by the E2 operator from two parents with training excess
0.624% and 0.674%, neither of which was the population best
at the time (0.513%). The child measured 0.543% before the
host step and 0.503% after it, became the new best, and was
retained unchanged to the final population.
The second is the individual selected at 400 total calls
by arm B on seed 86001; its training excess is 0.724% and
its sealed c100 excess 0.816%. It scores s(a) = (0.8 δ/a +
0.2 + [δ = 0]) π, where π = 0.7 if δ < 5 and 1 otherwise.
In addition, the score of the bin with the largest available
capacity is multiplied by 0.7 whenever some partially filled
bin can take the item with δ ≥5. On the same input
it also chooses the bin with 80. Both heuristics combine
mechanisms that the domain card names, best fit as a baseline
and small residuals as waste, into specific functional forms
and parameters. T-GADE’s contribution is this concretization,
combination, and parameterization under execution feedback,
not a new principle of bin packing.
The lineage of improvements shows how the retained pop-
ulation is used. For each generation of each run, we take the
minimum-energy child that improves on the history best, if
any. We then classify the parents given to the genetic operator
against the best of that generation’s parent population. A
parent counts as best when its energy equals the minimum
over that generation’s parents, and every parent tied at the
minimum counts as best. The shares below are pooled over
the 10 runs and are shown in the last column of Table IV.
At T = 0 only 3% of new-best events in the generational
family descend from parents other than the current best; at
T = 0.001, 0.003, and 0.01 the share is 52%, 53%, and 60%.
At T = 0.03 it is 36% and at T = 0.1 it is 52%, so the share
is high at intermediate temperatures and not monotone in T.
Retained non-best individuals are used as parents of the next
improvement, not merely stored. This is lineage evidence, not
a causal test. The host also consults information on the best
parent separately.


--- Page 10 ---
10
VII. DISCUSSION
A. Reading the two families through one objective
The same free energy produces two different temperature
responses, and the framework explains why. In the steady-state
Fermi-type family, exclusion by energy level already prevents
the population from collapsing, so the diversity term has no
collapse to repair; raising T trades quality for spread, and
quality degrades slowly. The level filter also runs before the
free-energy step, so a newcomer at the level of a retained
individual is removed before its features are compared. A
level-internal tie-break that keeps the candidate with the lower
FT is a natural refinement and would give T > 0 a role that
the present implementation does not offer. In the generational
Bose-type family, nothing but the diversity term keeps the pop-
ulation from becoming copies, so a small positive temperature
changes the dynamics qualitatively. It restores a population of
distinct survivors, and at intermediate temperatures more than
half of the subsequent improvements descend from non-best
survivors. The endpoint improves at T = 0.001–0.003 but not
at T = 0.01, so lineage use alone does not predict endpoint
gain. The useful temperatures are those whose copy penalty,
about 1240T percentage points, exceeds the objective spread
of a good population by about one order of magnitude; much
larger temperatures buy spread at the expense of quality. These
are statements about the two families as a whole, not about
their endpoints alone.
B. Zero temperature depends on the family
EoH’s survival rule is recovered at T = 0 in the steady-state
Fermi-type family, and in this experiment the host-equipped
steady-state Fermi-type configuration at T = 0 has the best
median of that family. The generational Bose-type family at
T = 0 is the predicted collapse and serves as the control of
that family. Comparing “T-GADE at T = 0” with “T-GADE
at T > 0” without naming the family is therefore not well
defined. The remaining two combinations, generational Fermi-
type and steady-state Bose-type with the host, remain open;
the present data do not separate the effect of occupancy from
the effect of the update scheme.
C. The host and its limits
T-GADE adds two instruments to the EoH survival rule: the
host and the temperature-controlled diversity term. Arm B is
the EoH survival rule at T = 0 with the host attached, so the
preregistered comparison isolates the host, and the diversity
term is assessed in the temperature-response experiments.
The host alone reads the training values and a hand-written
domain card and alone has the output limit of 8,192 tokens
in place of 2,048. It is common to every host-equipped arm,
so the temperature results are internal to the host-equipped
design. Part of its gain with gpt-oss-20b is the repair of
weak proposals, and the value of the host may depend on the
generator. The host accepts about 60% of its own revisions
under the keep-best rule. Equal calls are not equal cost: host-
equipped runs use about 1.7 times the tokens per call. This
structure separates the LLM call budgets for variation and local
improvement, while survival selection remains a free-energy
computation.
D. Choice of diversity features
The diversity feature is a design choice per problem, and
the behavior feature of Section IV-C is one choice. For text
artifacts, the Gram matrix of output embeddings is the natural
counterpart [20]. With a self-hosted open-weight generator, as
with gpt-oss-20b on vLLM here, the generator’s intermediate-
layer representation is a further candidate; it may reduce
task-specific feature design and makes the diversity term
available before execution. Individuals with identical behavior
but different internal representations then count as diverse, and
the useful range of the selection temperature, including the
1240T rule of thumb, must be revalidated for the new feature
geometry. Layer and pooling choices, normalization, context
dependence, and the cost of one extra forward pass remain
open design questions. Neither alternative was tested in this
paper.
E. Scope
The proposal of T-GADE does not restrict the artifact, the
evaluator, or the features; the evidence here is an implemen-
tation example on one task, one generator, and two families,
with ten seeds per arm. The task is close to saturation, with all
configurations ending within a fraction of a percentage point
of each other, so the sealed c100 differences at the endpoint
are small. The sealed c500 instances separate no arm. The
claims are the reach speed, the temperature responses, and the
generational favorable region. The reach speed was confirmed
by a preregistered primary comparison on sealed instances; the
temperature responses rest on paired tests of training values
and on auxiliary evaluation of sealed values. The quality gain
of the generational favorable region is confirmed on training
excess and remains a descriptive trend on the sealed c100
instances. In the steady-state Fermi-type family the endpoint
is best at T = 0, and there the temperature is a control of
spread, not a claimed source of endpoint gain. On this task,
which is close to saturation, the two instruments were not
both needed for quality: the host carried the reach-speed gain,
and the diversity term showed its value where a collapse had
to be undone. Tasks on which diversity is actively required
for quality, such as multimodal or deceptive objectives, are
the natural setting for the temperature term and remain future
work.
F. Toward adaptive temperature
The quality and diversity responses obtained at fixed tem-
peratures can inform the design of adaptive temperature con-
trol. The copy-penalty rule of thumb can calibrate the search
range, and the temperature may also be adjusted from the
observed diversity, as in Feedback TDGA [22]. Since the
log-determinant diversity of T-GADE is available at every
selection, such feedback control and temperature selection at
equal budget are future work.


--- Page 11 ---
11
VIII. CONCLUSION
We proposed T-GADE, an evolutionary computation frame-
work inspired by TDGA and extended with LLMs. T-GADE
takes artifacts generated by an LLM as individuals and has
LLM operators, the HoxLM, generational and steady-state up-
date schemes, and Fermi-type and Bose-type occupancy rules.
Under one free-energy objective, the selection temperature
controls diversity. The survival rule of EoH is the steady-state
Fermi-type point at zero temperature, and generational Bose-
type selection at zero temperature is a collapse to copies. We
tested an implementation example aligned with EoH on the on-
line bin-packing task. A seed-paired preregistered comparison
on sealed instances confirmed, as the primary endpoint, that
the host-equipped configuration reaches low excess with fewer
total LLM calls than EoH. The configuration is also better in
median, mean, and worst case. Temperature controls the spread
of the retained population in both families. In training quality
the generational Bose-type family is best at T = 0.001, with
a descriptive favorable region up to T = 0.003, while the
steady-state Fermi-type family has its best median at T = 0.
The evolved heuristics are readable scoring rules whose mech-
anisms and parameters were concretized under execution feed-
back. Future work includes the remaining occupancy–update
combinations, adaptive temperature through restart ensembles
across temperatures and entropy feedback, generalization of
the diversity feature to output embeddings and intermediate-
layer representations, richer structured artifacts, and tasks and
generators on which diversity is actively required for quality.
Code and preregistrations: https://github.com/o-ankomochi
-o/T-GADE.

ber JP23K11252.
APPENDIX A
TERMINOLOGY AND SYMBOLS
Table V lists the terms of this paper and Table VI the
symbols.
APPENDIX B
CALL ACCOUNTING AND ENDPOINTS
Each admitted LLM request consumes one budget unit,
including requests whose outputs cannot be parsed or evalu-
ated; transport retries are counted separately. In the steady-
state loop, operator calls are capped at 1,600 (3,200 for
EoH) and the host is called at most once per child, so the
recorded totals of the host-equipped runs lie between 3,175
and 3,197, and the EoH runs end at 3,200. In the generational
loop each generation plans 9 children and 9 host calls; a
failed operator call leaves a vacancy that is recorded, not
refilled, and the recorded totals lie between 3,158 and 3,185.
Evaluations of children before and after the host step and of
registered individuals execute code without LLM calls. The
budget-point selection uses only training values, and sealed
scoring runs once after all runs have finished. In the reach-
speed comparison the host-equipped runs ended at 792 to 799
total calls, that is, 400 operator calls plus fewer than 400 host
calls. The budget point at b sums, for each registration, the
operator and host requests started before it, and admits only
registrations with a sum of at most b. The scoring script used
for the reported results counts a run as having reached budget b
when its total calls reach b −1, that is, with one call of slack.
The two runs ending at 799 calls (seeds 86003 and 86007)
are therefore admitted at b = 800. This does not affect the
preregistered primary endpoint at 400 total calls, and the last
column of Table II is the endpoint of at most 800 calls.

TABLE V
TERMINOLOGY.
Term
Meaning
artifact
An LLM output with explicit structure; the substance of an individual. In this implementation, an explanation paired with code
energy
The value a task-specific evaluator assigns to an individual; lower is better. In this implementation, (6)
feature
A vector ϕℓthat measures differences between artifacts; designed per problem
population diversity
The spread H of a population computed from the features; in this paper the log-determinant of the Gram matrix
free energy
FT = ⟨E⟩−TH; the quantity that survival selection minimizes
selection temperature
The weight T of diversity; distinct from the LLM sampling temperature
occupancy
The rule for the number of individuals per level; Fermi-type permits at most one, Bose-type permits repetition
level
The equivalence class in which occupancy is counted; in this implementation the objective value rounded to five decimals
update scheme
Generational is short for the generational replacement model, steady-state for the steady-state model; the former replaces the
population as a whole, the latter one or a few individuals per step, one in T-GADE
operator
An LLM operator that generates children
HoxLM
An LLM that attempts self-repair after evaluation and before survival selection; the HoxLM of this implementation is called the
host
sealed instances
Evaluation instances never read during search; c100 and c500
budget point
The point at which the best training individual among registrations within b total calls is evaluated
excess ratio
The ratio of the bin-count excess to the lower bound, excess for short; lower is better
